Why a matching line beats a random mix

When your bag, earrings and headband come from the **same fabric**, you can sell them as a **set**. A customer who came for earrings may leave with a matching headband. You also waste less: the offcuts from a tote bag are the right size for earrings and covered buttons. And because you repeat the same few designs, you get faster and your quality becomes consistent, which is what makes customers come back.

**What she buys it for:** everyday use, owambe and events, gifts, uniforms for a group.

Words you need to know
**Interfacing:** a stiffening fabric ironed (fusible) or sewn onto the back of the main fabric. It makes a bag stand up and hold its shape instead of flopping.
**Lining:** the inside fabric of a bag. It hides raw seams and makes the bag look finished.
**Findings:** the small metal parts of jewellery: ear wires, studs, jump rings, clasps and crimp beads.
**Jump ring:** a small open metal ring that joins a charm or earring shape to an ear wire.
**Stretch cord:** elastic beading cord. Thicker cord is stronger; the bead holes must be big enough for the cord to pass, ideally twice.
**Seam allowance:** the strip of fabric between the cut edge and your stitch line, for example 1 cm. Keep it the same on every piece.
Quality checks before you pay
**Ankara:** look at both sides. Good wax print has a clear pattern and colour on the back as well. Rub a damp white cloth on a corner; if colour comes off heavily, it may bleed in the wash.
**Lining and interfacing:** choose a weight that suits the bag. Light interfacing for small purses, medium or heavy for totes.
**Thread:** use polyester thread for bags; it is stronger than most cheap cotton thread. Match or deliberately contrast the colour.
**Beads:** pour a few into your palm. Reject beads with chipped edges, uneven holes or flaking paint. Check that your cord fits through the hole.

**Findings:** ask what metal they are. Surgical stainless steel, titanium and sterling silver are less likely to irritate sensitive ears than unknown base metal. Never claim nickel-free unless the supplier confirms it.
**Buy enough of one batch:** fabric and beads change between batches. Buy enough of a print or bead colour for your planned set.

Accessory making looks gentle, but it uses heat, sharp blades, needles, glue and tiny parts. A tidy, safe workspace protects you, your children and your stock. It also makes you faster, because you are not searching for pliers or picking beads out of the rug.
A toolbox
A place for every tool keeps you safe and speeds up production.
Setting up your workspace
A table at a comfortable height with good light, ideally near a window by day and a bright bulb at night.
A tray or bead mat with raised edges so beads do not roll away.
Labelled containers for findings, beads by colour and fabric offcuts by print.
A heat-safe spot for the iron and glue gun, away from the table edge and from curtains.
A lidded box for everything small and sharp when you finish for the day.
Heat, blades and glue

Glue guns and irons cause burns: rest them on a stand, never on fabric, and unplug them when you leave the table. Cut away from your body and keep blades and needles in a closed box. Use strong solvent glues only with good air flow, follow the label, and keep them away from flames. If power goes off and comes back, check that irons and glue guns were switched off at the socket.
Children and small parts

Beads, buttons, jump rings and button batteries are choking hazards for young children. Work where toddlers cannot reach, sweep the floor after each session, and never sell beaded jewellery as a toy or for babies.
How many pieces can you really make?

**Production capacity** is the number of pieces you can make in a week at your normal quality, with your real life included: children, work, market days and power cuts. Customers forgive a lot, but not a promised order that arrives late. Measure your capacity from a timed trial, not from hope.
Choose one product and make three pieces, timing each one from start to finish, including cutting and finishing.
Take the average time. Ignore your first piece if it was much slower.
Count the hours you can honestly spend making each week.
Divide your weekly hours (in minutes) by the average time per piece.
Take away about one fifth for set-up, mistakes and interruptions.

Worked example: weekly capacity for earrings and bracelets
For example, Halima in Kano can spend about 10 hours a week on her accessories, around her family and her shop duties.
She times three pairs of covered-button earrings: 28, 22 and 20 minutes. She ignores the first and averages 21 minutes a pair.
She plans 6 of her 10 hours for earrings: 6 × 60 = 360 minutes. 360 ÷ 21 = about 17 pairs.
She removes about one fifth for interruptions: 17 × 0.8 = about 13 pairs.
She times stretch bracelets at about 15 minutes each. Her other 4 hours: 240 ÷ 15 = 16, then 16 × 0.8 = about 12 bracelets.
Halima can safely promise about 13 pairs of earrings and 12 bracelets a week. If a customer asks for 40 pairs for a wedding, she knows she needs about three weeks, or help.

Using capacity when you take orders

Your capacity figure becomes your promise to customers. When someone asks for a bulk order, such as aso-ebi earrings for a wedding party or 30 totes as staff gifts, divide the quantity by your weekly capacity to get the number of weeks, then add a few days for buying materials and for delivery. Tell the customer that date, not a hopeful one. Ask for a deposit on large or custom orders, commonly half, to cover materials before you start cutting, and write the agreed quantity, colours, price, deposit and delivery date in one WhatsApp message so both of you can refer back to it.

If an order is bigger than your capacity, you have three honest choices: give a later date, simplify the design so each piece takes less time, or bring in a trained helper who follows your recipe card. Never accept an order you cannot finish on time just to avoid saying no; one late wedding order can cost you many future referrals.

Wax-print ankara is usually a little over 110 cm wide, so these pieces fit comfortably in about 1 yard, often with offcuts left for earrings. Make **cardboard templates** of each piece once. Tracing round a template with chalk is faster and more accurate than measuring every time, and it makes every bag the same size.
Sewing steps
**Prepare.** Wash, dry and iron the ankara. Cut all pieces using your templates, keeping the print straight and centred on the front panel.

**Fuse the interfacing.** Place the glue side (rough, shiny side) on the wrong side of each outer panel. Cover with a damp cloth and press firmly with a hot iron for about 10 to 15 seconds in each spot. Lift and press; do not slide the iron. Follow the interfacing maker's instructions if they differ.

**Make the straps.** Fold each strap in half lengthwise and press. Open, fold both long edges in to meet the centre crease, press, then fold in half again so you have a strip about 2.5 cm wide. Topstitch close to both long edges.
**Sew the outer bag.** Place the two outer panels right sides together. Sew down one side, across the bottom and up the other side. Backstitch at the start and end of every seam.

**Box the corners.** At each bottom corner, pull the fabric apart so the side seam sits on top of the bottom seam, making a triangle. Measure 8 cm across the triangle, draw a line, sew along it twice, and trim the tip to 1 cm. This gives the bag a flat base.
**Sew the lining** the same way, but leave a gap of about 12 cm in the bottom seam for turning. Box its corners too.

**Attach the straps.** With the outer bag right side out, pin each strap end to the top edge, raw edges together, about 8 cm in from each side seam. Make sure the straps are not twisted. Stitch them in place inside the seam allowance.

**Join outer and lining.** Turn the lining wrong side out. Put the outer bag inside the lining so the right sides face each other and the straps are tucked between them. Match the side seams, pin all round the top, and sew.

**Turn and finish.** Pull the bag right side out through the gap in the lining. Push the lining down inside, roll the top seam so no lining shows, and press. Topstitch about 0.5 cm from the top edge. Close the lining gap by folding in its edges and stitching close to the edge.

Small accessories are where batching pays off most. Making one pair of earrings from start to finish, then the next, means picking up and putting down the same tools again and again. Doing **one step for all pieces** before moving on is faster and gives more even results. First, the methods.
A string of beads
A stretch bracelet is simple, but the cord, size and knot decide whether it lasts.
Stretch bracelets
**Measure the wrist** snugly with a tape measure, then add about 1 to 2 cm. Add more for big beads, because they take up space on the inside of the circle.
**Pre-stretch the cord.** Pull a length of stretch cord firmly several times. This stops it loosening after the customer wears it.
**Cut** the cord to the bracelet length plus about 10 cm at each end for tying. Clip one end with a bead stopper or binder clip.
**String your beads** in your planned pattern. Hold the strand round the wrist or a tape measure to check the size.
**Tie a surgeon's knot:** cross the ends and pass one through twice, pull, then cross back and pass through once more. Pull each side firmly so the knot tightens.
**Secure** the knot with a small dot of jewellery glue and let it dry fully before trimming the ends. Slide the knot inside a bead with a larger hole if you can.
Covered-button earrings
Cut fabric circles using the template that comes with your cover button kit. Centre a motif from the print in each circle; matching pairs matter.
Place the fabric face down in the rubber mould, press the button top in, tuck the fabric edges inwards, add the back and press it home with the pusher.
To hang the button: open a jump ring by **twisting the ends sideways**, one end towards you and one away. Never pull the ring open into an oval; it weakens the metal and will not close neatly.
Pass the open ring through the button shank and the loop of the ear wire, then twist it closed so the ends meet with no gap.
For stud earrings, remove or flatten the shank as the kit allows and glue on a flat-pad stud, following the glue's drying time.

A simple, saleable style is the **padded headband**: cut a strip of foam or wadding to the length of a plastic headband base, glue it on, wrap the base in an ankara strip cut on the bias (diagonally, so it stretches round curves), and glue the ends neatly inside. An **elastic-back headband** is sewn instead: a fabric tube for the front and a shorter tube with flat elastic for the back. Test sizes on several heads before you cut a batch, and write down the measurements that fit best.

Many makers price by guessing, or by copying the cheapest seller. Then they work for weeks and find they have earned almost nothing. Costing means knowing exactly what one piece costs you before you name a price. It needs only four parts: **materials, labour, overhead and profit**.
A paper receipt
Keep every receipt: your costing is only as accurate as your records.
What a price is built from
Profit
Overhead
Labour
Materials, labour and overhead make your cost; profit is added on top.
The four parts
**Materials:** everything that goes into one piece, including packaging and labels. Divide bulk prices by how many pieces they make.
**Labour:** your time is a cost. Choose a fair hourly rate for your skill and area, then multiply by the time per piece from your batch timings.

**Overhead:** costs of running the business shared across pieces: fuel or electricity, needles and blades, data for posting, transport to the market. Add up a month and divide by pieces made that month.
**Profit:** money for the business itself, to buy more stock, replace tools and grow. Many small sellers add something like 20 to 50% on top of cost; check what your market supports.
Your **cost** is materials plus labour plus overhead. Your **price** is cost plus profit. If you sell below cost, every sale makes you poorer, even if money is coming in.

For example, Ada in Enugu. All prices are approximate examples; use your own receipts.
Cover buttons: kit of 20 for about ₦6,000, so about ₦300 each, ₦600 for a pair.

Fabric offcut and glue: about ₦80. Earring card and small bag: about ₦150.

Labour: 12 minutes a pair in batches, at ₦1,500 an hour: 1,500 ÷ 60 × 12 = ₦300.
Overhead: about ₦6,000 a month across about 60 pieces = ₦100 a pair.
Cost: 1,020 + 300 + 100 = ₦1,420. Adding about 50% profit: about ₦2,130.
Ada prices the pair at ₦2,500, which is within the range she saw from similar sellers and leaves her a profit of about ₦1,080 a pair on top of her labour.

Some craft pricing guides suggest doubling your cost for a wholesale price and doubling again for retail. That leaves room for shops to take their share, but in many Nigerian markets it gives prices buyers will not pay. Use it as a ceiling to compare, not a rule, and always know your cost floor.

If a cost rises, update your costing sheet first, then decide whether to raise your price, change a material or accept a smaller profit for a while. Tell regular customers about a price change in advance; most will accept a fair, explained increase.

The way to guarantee that is a short, written finishing standard that you check every piece against before it goes on sale.

The inspection routine
Inspect in good daylight or under a bright white bulb, never in dim light.
Check each item against its standard, line by line, and look at it from the back as well as the front.
Give the piece a gentle stress test: tug each strap, stretch each bracelet a few times, give each ear wire a light pull.

What to do with seconds
Do not slip seconds in with full-price stock. Sell them clearly labelled as seconds at a lower price, use them as samples, or take them apart for materials. Honest seconds can still build goodwill.
Fix the cause, not just the piece

When the same defect shows up again and again, the problem is in your method, not your hands. Your defect notes show the pattern. Ask: at which step does this go wrong, and what change to the tool, template or step list would stop it?
Worked example: bracelets that come back broken
For example, Halima in Kano sold 30 stretch bracelets in a month. Four customers told her the bracelet snapped or came undone within two weeks.
She checks her defect notes and the returned pieces. Three of the four broke at the knot.
She realises she was using thin 0.5 mm cord for heavy glass beads, and trimming the ends before the glue was fully dry.
She changes her recipe card: 0.8 mm cord for beads 8 mm and above, pre-stretch every length, and trim only after the glue has dried for the time on its label.
She replaces the four bracelets free of charge and thanks each customer for telling her.
Next month she sells 35 bracelets and hears of one problem, caused by a cracked bead she now checks for.
A small change in materials and one rule on her recipe card cut breakages sharply, and the free replacements turned upset buyers into repeat customers.
Common defects and their usual causes
**Wavy topstitching:** sewing too fast or not using an edge guide. Slow down and use the machine plate guide or a tape line.
**Lining puffs:** different seam allowances on outer and lining. Mark one allowance on the machine.
**Fabric wrinkles on covered buttons:** circle cut too big or fabric too thick. Use the kit template and lighter fabric.
**Earrings that do not match:** motifs chosen one at a time. Cut circles in pairs from the same spot in the pattern repeat.
**Bracelet knot slips:** cord not pre-stretched, knot not pulled tight, or glue not dry before trimming.
Finishing touches that lift the price

Beyond passing your checks, a few small finishing habits make a piece feel worth more. Press every bag and headband before photographing or packing it; creases look careless. Clip loose threads with sharp scissors rather than pulling them, which can pucker a seam. Sew or glue a small woven or printed label with your brand name inside each bag. Mount earrings on a printed card with your name and WhatsApp number on the back, so the card advertises for you after the sale. These touches add only a small amount to your material cost, which you include in your costing, but buyers notice them at once and they support a higher price.

Honest selling, original design and customer safety
Describe materials truthfully without overclaiming
Tell the difference between inspiration and copying
Apply safety rules for skin contact, small parts and children
Handle customer details and money in ways that protect both sides

Trust is the real product in a small accessories business. Most of your buyers will come through people who already know you: friends, colleagues, church and mosque members, WhatsApp contacts. One misleading description can travel through those networks faster than any advert. This lesson covers four areas where honesty and care matter most.
A shield
Honest descriptions and safe products protect your customers and your name.
1. Describe materials truthfully
Say **what the material is**: "gold-tone ear wires", not "gold earrings", unless the metal is real gold and you can prove it.
Only claim **sterling silver, stainless steel or nickel-free** if your supplier's information confirms it.
Say **glass beads** or **acrylic beads**, not "crystal" or "gemstone", unless that is what they are.
Call ankara by what it is (for example "cotton wax print"). Do not name a fabric brand unless you know the fabric is from that brand.
If a piece is partly made from bought components, that is fine. Do not claim you made parts you bought.
2. Inspiration versus copying
Inspired or copied?
Inspired (fine)
Copied (avoid)
Using a common technique like covered buttons
Following a general trend in shapes or colours
Learning from a tutorial, then designing your own
Reproducing another seller's distinctive signature design
Using her product photos as your own
Putting a designer brand's logo on your bags
Techniques and trends are shared; another maker's identifiable design, photos and brand logos are not yours to use.

Putting a famous fashion brand's logo or pattern on your work makes it a counterfeit, even if you made it by hand. It can lead to your posts being removed and to legal trouble, and it tells buyers your brand is not good enough on its own. Build your own recognisable look instead: your colour choices, your label, your packaging.
3. Safety for the wearer
Skin, small parts and children

Nickel is a common cause of skin allergy from jewellery; offer earrings on findings with a confirmed metal such as surgical stainless steel, titanium or sterling silver for sensitive ears. Beaded jewellery and small parts can choke babies and young children: do not make or sell them for that age group, and say 'not suitable for young children' where it applies. Check that clasps, knots and jump rings are secure so pieces do not fall apart in use.
Give simple care instructions: keep jewellery dry, remove before bathing or swimming, hand wash ankara bags gently in cold water and dry in shade.
For headbands, finish inside edges so no sharp plastic or hard glue lumps press on the head.
If a customer reports irritation, advise her to stop wearing the item and offer a replacement on different findings.
4. Protecting customers and yourself with money and data
Only collect the customer details you need: name, phone number and delivery address.
Do not post screenshots of chats or receipts that show customers' names, numbers or addresses without hiding them.
Confirm payment in your own bank or wallet app before sending goods. Screenshots and SMS alerts can be faked.
Agree price, delivery fee, delivery time and your return or replacement policy in writing (a WhatsApp message is enough) before taking payment.
Treat every buyer the same: one price list, one standard, whether she orders one pair or fifty.
Worked example: rewriting a misleading listing
For example, Ngozi had this WhatsApp status: "Luxury gold crystal earrings, original, hypoallergenic, ₦3,000." She checks her materials.
Her ear wires are gold-tone plated base metal; the supplier does not state the metal. So she removes "gold" and "hypoallergenic".
The stones are glass beads, not crystal. She changes "crystal" to "glass bead".
"Original" means nothing to the buyer, so she replaces it with what is true: "handmade in Aba".
She adds an option: the same design on surgical stainless steel ear wires for ₦500 more, because her new supplier confirms the metal.

New text: "Handmade ankara and glass bead drop earrings, gold-tone ear wires, ₦3,000. Sensitive ears? Ask for surgical stainless steel ear wires, ₦3,500." It is honest and still attractive, and it gives the buyer a choice.
A simple returns and replacement policy

Decide your policy before the first complaint, not during it. A fair policy for small accessories might be: if an item arrives damaged or fails because of how it was made (for example a strap seam opens or a bracelet knot slips) within a stated period such as 14 days, you repair or replace it free. Items damaged by misuse, or earrings that have been worn, are not returnable for hygiene reasons, and you say so clearly. Ask the customer for a photo of the problem first. Write the policy in your catalogue description and on your thank-you card so it is agreed before payment.

Handled calmly, a complaint is a chance to show your standards. Reply quickly, thank the customer, fix the problem, and note the cause in your defect record from Lesson 3.1. Many of your most loyal buyers will be people whose problem you solved well.

Online, the photo is the product. A buyer on WhatsApp or Instagram cannot touch your bag, so the picture must show its colour, size, finishing and how it looks in use, honestly. You do not need a professional camera. A clean phone, daylight and a plain background are enough for strong product photos.
A person photographing a product
Daylight, a plain background and a steady phone are most of good product photography.
Simple set-up
**Clean the lens** with a soft cloth. A greasy lens makes every photo hazy.
**Use daylight from a window**, not direct sun. Bright, soft light shows true colours; direct sun makes harsh shadows. Turn off room bulbs, which add a yellow or blue tint.
**Use a plain background**: white card, a plain cloth or a clean wooden table. Keep the same background for all your products so your page looks like one brand.
**Bounce light into shadows** with a white card or sheet of paper held opposite the window.
**Hold the phone steady**: rest your elbows on the table or lean the phone on a cup. Tap the screen on the item to focus, and do not use digital zoom; move closer instead.
**Do not use filters** that change the colours. Light edits to brightness are fine, but the buyer must receive what she saw.

Common scams

Fake payment alerts, buyers who 'overpay' and ask for a refund of the difference, and messages offering paid 'verification' or 'promotion' of your page are common tricks. Confirm every payment in your own bank or wallet app, never refund an overpayment until the full amount has cleared in your account, and never share one-time passwords or PINs.
Delivery and packaging

Worked example: a church fair pop-up (figures approximate)

She shows a printed card with her account details and WhatsApp number, and checks each transfer in her app before handing over goods.
She sells 14 pairs of earrings, 9 bracelets and 3 sets: 14 × 2,500 + 9 × 2,000 + 3 × 8,000 = ₦77,000.
She collects 11 phone numbers from buyers who agree to receive her new stock updates.
After the table fee, transport and the cost of the pieces sold, she knows her real profit for the day, and she has 11 new contacts for repeat sales.
Selling through boutiques
**Wholesale:** the shop buys your pieces outright at a lower price and resells them. You are paid at once.

**Consignment:** the shop displays your pieces and pays you only when they sell, minus its share. Agree the share, payment dates, retail price and what happens to unsold or damaged stock, in writing, and keep a signed list of every piece you leave.

Use a notebook, a free spreadsheet app such as Google Sheets, or a simple bookkeeping app. Keep a **stock count** too: how many of each item you made and how many are left. Write one line per sale on the day, not from memory at the end of the month.
Three numbers to work out every month
**Profit per product:** (price minus cost) × quantity sold. This shows which products really earn money, not just which bring in the most cash.
**Sell-through:** pieces sold ÷ pieces made × 100. A product with 80% sell-through is in demand; 20% means it is sitting.
**Repeat customers:** how many buyers this month had bought before. Repeat buying is the strongest sign your quality is right.

Sell-through (low to high)
Plotting each product by how fast it sells and how much it earns shows where to put your time.

Read the matrix like this: high sell-through and high profit means **make more**. High sell-through but low profit means people want it but you earn too little, so **fix the price or cost**. Low sell-through and high profit may need **new versions** (colours, sizes, better photos). Low on both means **drop or redesign**.
Worked example: one month of records
For example, Funmi's log for September shows four products. Figures are illustrative.
Covered-button earrings: made 30, sold 26, profit ₦1,080 each. Sell-through 26 ÷ 30 = 87%. Profit 26 × 1,080 = ₦28,080.
Lined totes: made 8, sold 6, profit ₦5,000 each. Sell-through 75%. Profit ₦30,000.
Padded headbands: made 10, sold 3, profit ₦1,500 each. Sell-through 30%. Profit ₦4,500.
Large beaded statement bracelets: made 10, sold 8, profit ₦200 each because they take 50 minutes. Sell-through 80%. Profit ₦1,600.
Earrings and totes are 'make more'. Statement bracelets sell well but earn too little, so she raises their price or simplifies the design. Headbands sit, so she asks buyers why before making more.
Getting feedback that helps
"Do you like it?" gets polite answers. Ask specific questions a few days after delivery, by WhatsApp or in person:

Is there anything you would change: size, colour, length, closure?
What would you pay for a version with a zip or matching earrings?
Have you worn or used it yet, and how has it held up?
Separate the three causes

When a product does not sell, decide which of three causes it is before acting: quality (customers see a flaw), price (they like it but say it is too costly) or fit (it is not their style). Each needs a different fix, and your feedback answers tell you which one it is.
Is the business making money?

Sales are not profit. At the end of each month, add up all sales income, then take away the cost of the pieces you sold (from your cost column) and any extra spending not already in your costing, such as stall fees, adverts or a new tool. What is left is your real monthly profit. Keep business money separate from household money, even if only by using a separate wallet account such as an Opay or Moniepoint account just for the business. That way you can see clearly whether the business is paying for its own materials, and you avoid using next month's fabric money for daily expenses.
Total sales income for the month.
Minus the cost of the pieces you sold.
Minus extra costs not in your costing: stall fees, adverts, new tools.
The result is your monthly profit. Compare it with last month.

Review your log at the same time each month, for example the first Sunday, and write three lines: what sold best, what did not, and one change for next month. Over three months those notes show trends that a single good or bad week hides, such as earrings selling more before festive seasons or totes selling best when schools resume.

This last lesson pulls everything together into your capstone: a small, consistent collection, honest presentation, real selling and a plan for the next 90 days. The certificate means most when it rests on actual sales attempts, even small ones, rather than craft skill alone.
A woman planning her business at a board

What your sales project contains
**Collection:** at least two core products, in a batch of matching pieces, all passing your finishing standard.
**Costing sheets:** the four-part costing and final price for each product.
**Presentation:** the five standard photos and six-part description for each product, posted on at least one channel.

A 90-day plan in three blocks
Days 1 to 30: focus
Days 31 to 60: grow
Days 61 to 90: review
Each month has one main job, so the plan stays realistic around family and work.
Writing the 90-day plan
**Days 1 to 30, focus:** make more of your 'make more' products, fix one costing or quality problem, and set a sales target based on last month's numbers.
**Days 31 to 60, grow:** add one channel (for example a pop-up or one boutique on consignment) or one tested new design, not both.
**Days 61 to 90, review:** compare profit, sell-through and repeat customers with your starting month; drop what is not working.
Write each step with a number and a date, for example "make 40 pairs of earrings by 30 November", not "make more earrings".
Pitching to a shop or mentor

When you approach a boutique, a gift shop or a mentor, specific results speak louder than "my work is beautiful". Prepare a one-page sheet and a short spoken pitch that covers what you make, proof that people buy it, what it costs the shop, and how reliably you can supply.
Worked example: Funmi's pitch to a boutique
For example, Funmi visits a boutique in Ibadan that sells women's wear but has few accessories.

Supply: "I can deliver 20 pairs and 4 totes every two weeks, all checked against my finishing standard."
Offer: "Would you try 10 pairs and 2 totes on consignment for one month, with terms in writing?"
The owner agrees to a one-month consignment trial. Funmi writes the share, payment date and returns policy on a signed stock list.
Be honest about your size

A small, well-run business is something to present with confidence. Say exactly how many pieces you can supply and how long orders take. Overpromising volume is the quickest way to lose a shop's trust.

Your reflection is short, half a page is enough, but it should be specific and honest. Answer four questions in your own words. What did you make, and how consistent was it? Free replacements for each buyer
For example, Halima in Kano sold 30 stretch bracelets in a month. Four customers said theirs snapped or came undone within two weeks.
She checked her notes. Three of the four broke at the knot.
She was using thin 0.5 mm cord for heavy glass beads, and trimming the ends before the glue was dry.
So she changed her recipe card: 0.8 mm cord for beads 8 mm and above, pre-stretch every length, and trim only after the glue has dried.
She replaced the four bracelets free and thanked each customer. Next month she sold 35 and heard of only one problem.

Name materials exactly. For example, Ngozi changed her listing to say gold-tone ear wires, glass beads, and handmade in Aba.
She removed gold, crystal and hypoallergenic, because her supplier could not confirm them. Never claim a metal or stone you cannot confirm.
And never put a famous brand's logo on your work. That makes it a counterfeit, even if you made it by hand.
Safety first
Protect the wearer and the buyer
Nickel can cause skin allergy. Offer confirmed metals: surgical stainless steel, titanium or sterling silver.
Beads and small parts can choke. Do not make or sell them for babies and young children.
Confirm payment in your own bank or wallet app. Screenshots and SMS alerts can be faked.

Nickel is a common cause of skin allergy from jewellery. Offer earrings on confirmed metals for sensitive ears. If a customer reports irritation, advise her to stop wearing it, and offer a replacement on different findings.
Beaded jewellery and small parts can choke babies and young children. Do not sell for that age group, and say not suitable for young children where it applies.
And confirm payment in your own app before sending goods, because screenshots and SMS alerts can be faked. Agree price, delivery and your replacement policy in writing first.
Photo set-up
Good photos with just a phone
Clean the lens
Window daylight, not direct sun
Plain background, same every time
White card to bounce light
Steady phone, no digital zoom

You do not need a professional camera. Clean the lens with a soft cloth. Use daylight from a window, not direct sun. Use a plain background, the same for every product.
Hold a white card opposite the window to lift shadows. Keep the phone steady, and move closer instead of zooming.
And use no filters that change colours. The buyer must receive what she saw.

Three numbers every month
Log every sale on the day
Profit per product: price minus cost, times qty
Sell-through: sold ÷ made × 100
Repeat customers
Write one line per sale on the day: date, product, quantity, price, cost, channel and customer's first name. Keep a stock count too.
Each month, work out profit per product: price minus cost, times the number sold. That shows what really earns money.
Then sell-through: pieces sold, divided by pieces made, times 100. 80 percent means it is in demand. 20 percent means it is sitting.
And count repeat customers. Repeat buying is the strongest sign your quality is right.
